passage: At the edge of the municipal pool in Lajpat Nagar, Tarun gripped the railing so hard his knuckles went pale. The water smelled of chlorine and echoed with other children's shouts. 'It's dangerous,' he told Anand sir, the swimming coach. 'It's too deep. Someone will drown.' 'This end is only up to your chest,' Anand sir said, standing in it to show him. Tarun shook his head. 'But I feel it. My tummy's all wobbly. That means it's not safe.' Anand sir climbed out and sat on the step beside him. 'Your tummy is telling you something new is happening. Shall we just sit with our feet in today?' Tarun lowered one foot, then the other. The water was warm.

qa.a: Anand sir said this end is only up to Tarun's chest.

qa.a: Anand sir named the feeling as a sign of something new, not danger, and offered a tiny step, feet in the water, so Tarun could test the pool slowly.

qa.q: What would change if Anand sir had said, 'Don't be silly, jump in'?
qa.a: Tarun would likely feel more scared and ashamed, and the idea that the feeling proves danger would grow instead of being gently tested.

'I'm not going.' Amandeep sat on the stairs with his swimming bag upside down.
'Why?' Jatin asked, pulling on his shoes.
'The pool is dangerous.'
'Who said?'
'Me. My heart is going boom-boom-boom. That means it's dangerous.'
'Your heart went boom-boom-boom before your birthday party too. Was the party dangerous?'
Amandeep frowned. 'That was a happy boom.'
'Feels the same from inside, na?'
'...A bit.'
Mummy called from the kitchen, 'Jatin, is he ready?'
'Almost!' Jatin sat down on the step. 'Veerji will stay at the side the whole time. You can wave at me every length.'
'Every length?'
'Every single one.'
Amandeep picked the bag up and turned it the right way round.

qa.a: Amandeep sat on the stairs with his swimming bag upside down.

qa.q: Why does Amandeep think the pool is dangerous?
qa.a: Amandeep's heart is pounding, and to him that strong feeling seems to prove the pool is unsafe, even though nothing about the pool has changed.

qa.q: Which of Jatin's questions was the turning point, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether the birthday party was dangerous helped Amandeep notice that the same boom can come with happy or new things, so the feeling isn't proof of danger.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin to be the one getting Amandeep to class?
qa.a: Jatin is juggling his own shoes and Mummy's call, yet sits down and offers to stay at the side, which shows he cares more about Amandeep feeling safe than about rushing.

grounding: Shows a child who takes his pounding heart as proof that the pool is dangerous, and an elder brother who gently questions it.

passage: My name is Afreen and I am nine. Last summer, before my first swimming class, I told Abbu the pool was too dangerous for children. I was very sure. My legs felt shaky and my mouth was dry, and I thought that meant the pool was bad. When we got there, I would not take my slippers off. Jagdish uncle, the teacher, didn't make me. He gave me a float and let me walk on the steps. The next week I walked on the steps again, and the week after that I floated with his hand under me. Now I think the scared feeling was about me being new, not about the water. The pool was the same pool the whole time.

qa.a: Jagdish uncle gave Afreen a float.

qa.a: Afreen's legs felt shaky and mouth was dry, and those strong feelings seemed like proof that the pool itself was dangerous.

qa.q: What choice by Jagdish uncle made the change possible?
qa.a: Jagdish uncle didn't force Afreen in but let the steps come slowly, walking, then floating, so the feeling could fade while Afreen found out the water was safe.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt hearing that the pool was too dangerous for children?
qa.a: Abbu might have been worried and unsure whether to push, while hoping a gentle teacher could help Afreen try.

grounding: Shows a child looking back on taking shaky legs and a dry mouth as proof that a pool was dangerous before a first class.

passage:
Swim coach's note, summer beginners, Day 2

Vijay, 8, again would not come past the second step. He told me the pool is "dangerous". When I showed him the shallow end only reaches his waist, he said, "But my heart is beating super fast. So it IS dangerous."

I didn't argue with the feeling. I said a fast heart means his body knows something new is happening. Then I asked if he'd sit on the edge with his feet in. He did, gripping my sleeve.

By the end he was splashing, and he laughed when Sarita, from his group, kicked water at him. He still believes the pool is dangerous. But he stayed.

Next step: tomorrow he'll walk along the shallow end holding the edge. I'll tell his father what helped.

— Coach

qa.q: How far does the shallow end reach on Vijay?
qa.a: It only reaches his waist.

qa.q: Why does Vijay think his fast heartbeat proves the pool is dangerous?
qa.a: The feeling is so strong that it seems like information about the pool itself. To him, feeling scared and being in danger seem like the same thing.

qa.q: What choice did the coach make that helped Vijay stay?
qa.a: The coach didn't argue with the feeling but explained it as a sign of something new, then offered a small, safe step: feet in the water. That let Vijay test the pool without being pushed.

qa.q: How might Sarita have helped, even without meaning to?
qa.a: Kicking water at Vijay turned the pool into a place for a game, and he laughed. Seeing a child his age having fun may have made it feel less dangerous.

grounding: A coach notes a boy who feels nervous in a new swimming class and insists the pool is dangerous, taking the strength of his feeling as proof.

Dear Diary,

It's Lokesh. Tomorrow is the first swimming class at camp and I am NOT going. The pool is dangerous. I know because when I think about it my hands go cold and my tummy flips. If it wasn't dangerous, why would my body do that?

Baljeet says it's fun and he already swims in the deep end. Baljeet is not scared, so Baljeet does not know.

Mummy said, "The teacher will be in the water the whole time, my brave boy, and you can hold the rope." I said the rope could break.

My list of dangers: 1. Deep water. 2. Slippery floor. 3. My tummy.

It's 9 o'clock and my tummy is still flipping. That proves it.

Maybe I'll just sit on the side. Not swim.

qa.q: What did Mummy say Lokesh could hold?
qa.a: She said, "you can hold the rope."

qa.q: Why does Lokesh put "My tummy" on his list of dangers?
qa.a: To Lokesh, the flipping tummy feels like a warning about the pool, so it counts as a danger. The stronger the feeling, the more certain he is that the pool is unsafe.

qa.q: What would you advise Lokesh about tomorrow?
qa.a: Going to sit on the side is a good first step, and he could watch whether anything bad actually happens. Noticing that the tummy flips even when he's safe helps show feelings aren't proof.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel if Lokesh said Baljeet doesn't know anything because he isn't scared?
qa.a: Baljeet might feel brushed off, since he wanted to share something fun. He might also want to show Lokesh around the shallow end.

grounding: A boy nervous about his first swimming class decides the pool must be dangerous because his body feels scared, treating the feeling as proof.
